This guide is the shared machine reference for Codex, Claude Code, and Antigravity. The tools are installed once for the Windows user and are not duplicated inside each AI runtime.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Installed tools and locations\\r\\n\\r\\nWinGet package directories are versioned/managed by WinGet. Prefer calling the command by name through PATH. These paths confirm where the current packages live; a later package update may change a folder name.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Command | Current version | Current executable |\\r\\n|---|---|---|\\r\\n| `uv` | 0.12.23 | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\\\\Microsoft\\\\WinGet\\\\Packages\\\\astral-sh.uv_Microsoft.Winget.Source_8wekyb3d8bbwe\\\\uv.exe` |\\r\\n| `yt-dlp` | 2026.08.19 | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\\\\Microsoft\\\\WinGet\\\\Packages\\\\yt-dlp.yt-dlp_Microsoft.Winget.Source_8wekyb3d8bbwe\\\\yt-dlp.exe` |\\r\\n| `ffmpeg`, `ffprobe`, `ffplay` | N-126374-g089a48eb36-20260831 | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\\\\Microsoft\\\\WinGet\\\\Packages\\\\yt-dlp.FFmpeg_Microsoft.Winget.Source_8wekyb3d8bbwe\\\\ffmpeg-N-126374-g089a48eb36-win64-gpl\\\\bin\\\\` |\\r\\n| `deno` | 2.9.7 | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\\\\Microsoft\\\\WinGet\\\\Packages\\\\DenoLand.Deno_Microsoft.Winget.Source_8wekyb3d8bbwe\\\\deno.exe` |\\r\\n\\r\\nThe saved Windows user PATH already contains these package directories. All four commands were verified by name after reloading PATH. The original failure was a stale PATH inherited by already-running Codex, not a missing install. Restarting an AI application gives its new terminals the refreshed environment.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Check access in any runtime\\r\\n\\r\\nRun in that runtime\'s PowerShell terminal:\\r\\n\\r\\n```powershell\\r\\nGet-Command uv, yt-dlp, ffmpeg, ffprobe, ffplay, deno -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |\\r\\n  Select-Object Name, Source\\r\\nuv --version\\r\\nyt-dlp --version\\r\\nffmpeg -version | Select-Object -First 1\\r\\nffprobe -version | Select-Object -First 1\\r\\ndeno --version | Select-Object -First 1\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nIf the commands are installed but are not found, first refresh only the current PowerShell process from the saved Windows PATH:\\r\\n\\r\\n```powershell\\r\\n$machinePath = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable(\'Path\', \'Machine\')\\r\\n$userPath = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable(\'Path\', \'User\')\\r\\n$env:Path = \\"$userPath;$machinePath\\"\\r\\nGet-Command uv, yt-dlp, ffmpeg, ffprobe, ffplay, deno\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nIf that works, restart the affected AI application so its future terminals inherit the environment. Do not reinstall the tools or change persistent PATH just because one already-open shell cannot see them. If the refreshed shell still cannot find a command, inspect `winget list --id <package-id> --exact` and the executable at the table\'s current package path before making changes.\\r\\n\\r\\n## What each tool is for\\r\\n\\r\\n- `uv` creates and manages isolated Python project environments and dependencies. Use `uv add package-name` from the intended code project when that project should depend on a library; do not install every library globally. Use `uv run ...` to run a command in that project environment.\\r\\n- `yt-dlp` retrieves available video metadata and captions, and can retrieve media when specifically needed. For a first caption check, use `yt-dlp --list-subs <URL>`; use `--skip-download` when retrieving subtitles only. Do not assume a website exposes captions or that a successful install grants account access.\\r\\n- `ffmpeg` converts, trims, extracts and processes audio/video. `ffprobe` inspects media metadata. `ffplay` plays media for inspection.\\r\\n- `deno` is a JavaScript/TypeScript runtime. yt-dlp detects it as its JavaScript challenge runtime for supported YouTube extraction; ordinary tasks do not need to invoke it directly.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Python library scope\\r\\n\\r\\nPython packages installed in one interpreter are not automatically shared with the others. Codex\'s managed Python bundle includes `pypdf`, `pdfplumber`, `Pillow`, and `lxml`; the regular user Python 3.12 includes `requests`. Claude Code and Antigravity projects should check their own interpreter and project lockfile. Add only required missing packages to that project\'s isolated environment with uv. Do not modify Codex\'s managed runtime or put virtual environments in the Obsidian vault.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Instructions for the three AI tools\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Codex:** repository rules are in `AGENTS.md`. Use the shared CLI paths and PATH recovery above; restart Codex when its inherited PATH is stale.\\r\\n- **Claude Code:** repository rules are in `CLAUDE.md`. Use the same user-installed executables; project Python dependencies belong in that project\'s environment.\\r\\n- **Antigravity:** workspace rules are in `GEMINI.md` and `AGENTS.md`. Use the same user-installed executables; if it cannot see them, refresh/restart its terminal/application before considering an install.\\r\\n\\r\\nThese tools are shared at the Windows user level. Do not create copies in `.agents/`, `.claude/`, `.gemini/`, or inside the vault. Per-project Python packages remain isolated in each project\'s environment.\\r\\n"}'}]

Marks finished tasks done (struck through) in the task ledger, refreshes the handoff cache, and appends to the log. Trigger with /wrapup.\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\nClose the current LSAT U / Aspiring Attorneys session. Leave the next session a clean, accurate handoff and mark completed work as done so it is never re-run. Resolve the vault root from the current workspace and its nearest instruction files; never assume a saved `~/ai-os/`, Windows, or Mac path. In this vault, read `system/schema/llm-wiki.md` and obey its index/log conventions.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Step 0: read the anchor\\r\\n\\r\\nBefore writing anything, re-read `wiki/tasks.md` and `wiki/hot.md` so the handoff reflects the real goal, not just the last thing touched. If a `plans/` file or README framed this session, skim it too.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Step 1: confirm task status changes only when needed\\r\\n\\r\\nFrom verified session work, determine whether task status changes are needed. If no task status changes are needed, leave `wiki/tasks.md` alone and continue with the authorized handoff and log updates without a confirmation step. If task status changes are proposed, show Joshua the concrete proposal before editing `wiki/tasks.md`:\\r\\n\\r\\n```\\r\\nProposing for wiki/tasks.md:\\r\\n  -> Done (strike through): <items you believe are finished this session>\\r\\n  -> Stays in Now: <still in progress>\\r\\n  -> New Next: <anything surfaced that should be queued>\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nWait for Joshua to approve or correct proposed task status changes, unless those exact changes were already approved in this session. Completion MUST be correct: a wrong \\"Done\\" is the exact failure this prevents. Do not mark something done on a guess; if unsure, leave its status unchanged and say so. This gate applies to task status changes, not to routine authorized handoff/log filing. If requesting approval, explain that this skill requires confirmation before changing task status.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Step 2: write the authorized handoff and log\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **`wiki/tasks.md`** - move approved finished items into `## Done`, wrapping each in `~~...~~` with a date, e.g. `~~Wire AI tutor into official drill surface~~ (2026-06-12)`. Update `## Now` and `## Next` only as approved. Preserve older task records; do not prune or delete them without explicit authorization. Skip this file when no task changes were approved or needed.\\r\\n2. **`wiki/hot.md`** - rewrite the `## Most recent (YYYY-MM-DD): <title>` block with 4 to 8 bullets of what changed. Refresh `## Active priorities` and `## Open threads` so they are true now.\\r\\n3. **`wiki/log.md`** - append a new entry at the BOTTOM of the log using `## [YYYY-MM-DD] system | Session wrapup`. Include source/output links, meaningful changed pages, verified results, unresolved work, and any skipped steps. Use Joshua\'s client date/time context. Preserve old entries exactly, including their legacy formats; never rewrite or reorder them. Multiple sessions per day are normal, so add a distinct title suffix when useful. Or you might not be a student at all. Both are possible. Without law-school enrollment, this conditional doesn\'t tell us whether you\'re a student.</p>\\r\\n          <p>That\'s the difference: <strong>being enrolled guarantees being a student; not being enrolled leaves the question open.</strong></p>\\r\\n        </section>\\r\\n\\r\\n        <SufficientConditionExperience/>\\r\\n\\r\\n        <p>Want to see the relationship in a short video? These optional clips use a hypothetical student, Maya. The first supposes she is enrolled in law school. The second supposes only that she is a student. Compare what each piece of information establishes.</p>\\r\\n        <SufficientConditionFilm key=\\"sufficient-definition\\"/>\\r\\n\\r\\n        <section className=\\"cr-sufficient-explanation sc-indicator-list\\" aria-label=\\"Group 1 indicator words\\">\\r\\n          <h3>Group 1: Sufficient-condition indicators</h3>\\r\\n          <p>You\'ve seen how <strong>if</strong> points to the sufficient condition. These indicator words and phrases can help you recognize it too:</p>\\r\\n          <ul>{sufficientFamily.map(entry => <li key={entry.word}>{entry.word}</li>)}</ul>\\r\\n          <p>An <strong>indicator</strong> is a word or phrase that helps you recognize the relationship. In our example, <strong>if</strong> is the indicator; <strong>being enrolled in law school</strong> is the condition that guarantees being a student. Look for the words, then ask what they tell you about the two conditions.</p>\\r\\n        </section>\\r\\n\\r\\n        <section className=\\"cr-sufficient-explanation cr-sufficient-checks\\" aria-label=\\"Check your understanding of sufficiency\\">\\r\\n          <h3>Use an indicator to find the guarantee</h3>\\r\\n          <p>Let\'s use <strong>every</strong> in a new example:</p>\\r\\n          <blockquote><strong>Every</strong> applicant invited to an interview receives an email.</blockquote>\\r\\n          <ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"Which condition guarantees receiving an email?\\" options={[\'Being an applicant invited to an interview.\', \'Being an applicant.\']} correct={0} feedback={[\'Every covers the applicants invited to an interview. For anyone in that group, receiving an email is guaranteed.\', \'The rule covers applicants invited to an interview, not all applicants. Keep invited to an interview with applicant; that is what guarantees the email.\']}/>\\r\\n          <h3>What does the rule leave open?</h3>\\r\\n          <ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"Does this rule tell us whether applicants who aren\'t invited receive an email?\\" options={[\'Yes. They cannot receive an email.\', \'No. They could receive an email, or they might not.\']} correct={1} feedback={[\'The rule guarantees an email for invited applicants. It does not say that only invited applicants receive emails. Others could receive a different email, or no email at all.\', \'The rule tells us what invited applicants receive. It says nothing about emails to other applicants, so either possibility fits.\']}/>\\r\\n        </section>\\r\\n        <aside className=\\"cr-sufficient-bridge\\"><h3>Next: The Necessary Condition</h3><p>We\'ve focused on what guarantees being a student: enrollment in law school. Now look at the relationship from the other side. You can\'t be enrolled in law school without being a student. Being a student is the <strong>necessary condition</strong>, the part that must be true. That\'s what we\'ll examine next.</p></aside>\\r\\n      </div>\\r\\n      <p>Next, we\'ll examine what the sufficient condition requires.</p>\\r\\n    </ReferenceStep>\\r\\n\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={3} label=\\"The sufficient family\\" title=\\"Different words can preserve the same rule\\">\\r\\n      <p>An <strong>indicator</strong> is an expression that helps you recognize a conditional relationship. These expressions can introduce an idea that is enough to establish another.</p>\\r\\n      <p>For the next examples, use a different stated rule: anyone who borrows a locker has a key. We will express that same connection in several ways. We haven\'t said everyone with a key borrows a locker.</p>\\r\\n      <WordFamily entries={sufficientFamily} role=\\"sufficient\\"/>\\r\\n      <p>When/whenever and any/anytime group related forms together. An ending changes the kind of case being discussed, but these examples keep the same connection. For example, every guest wearing a blue badge covers that whole group. Guest alone would include people without badges. Use the expression to find the group, then keep the words that limit it.</p>\\r\\n      <ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"Every guest wearing a blue badge receives a lunch voucher. Which complete idea is enough?\\" options={[\'Guest\', \'Guest wearing a blue badge\', \'Receives a lunch voucher\']} correct={1} feedback={[\'Guest alone drops the badge restriction and would make a claim about unbadged guests.\', \'The rule gives a voucher to every guest wearing a blue badge. It has not said every voucher recipient wears a blue badge.\']}/>\\r\\n      <details className=\\"cr-extension\\"><summary>Two more Group 1 expressions</summary><p><strong>Where</strong> can state a relationship across locations: “Where a collection point operates, parcels can be returned.” An operating collection point establishes the availability of returns there. Availability is not proof that someone made a return.</p><p><strong>The only</strong> needs its complete phrase: “The only notebooks on this shelf are hardback.” A notebook on the shelf is hardback. The sentence does not put every hardback notebook there.</p><p>These are part of your Group 1 work. Here are the members of the necessary family:</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<table>\\r\\n  <thead><tr><th>Necessary Indicators</th><th>Example</th></tr></thead>\\r\\n  <tbody>\\r\\n    <tr><td>then</td><td><em>If I’m breathing, then air is present.</em></td></tr>\\r\\n    <tr><td>must</td><td><em>Air must be present for breathing.</em></td></tr>\\r\\n    <tr><td>necessary</td><td><em>Air is necessary for breathing.</em></td></tr>\\r\\n    <tr><td>required</td><td><em>Air is required for breathing.</em></td></tr>\\r\\n    <tr><td>only (if)</td><td><em>Only the presence of air allows for breathing.</em><br><br><em>I’m breathing, only if air is present.</em></td></tr>\\r\\n    <tr><td>depends</td><td><em>Breathing depends on air being present.</em></td></tr>\\r\\n    <tr><td>need (to)</td><td><em>I need air to breathe.</em></td></tr>\\r\\n    <tr><td>have to</td><td><em>I have to have air, if I’m breathing.</em></td></tr>\\r\\n    <tr><td>essential</td><td><em>Air is essential for breathing.</em></td></tr>\\r\\n    <tr><td>precondition</td><td><em>Air is a precondition for breathing.</em></td></tr>\\r\\n  </tbody>\\r\\n</table>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Notice the similarities in each of these words. text(await tools.apply_patch("*** Begin Patch\n*** Update File: C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp/src/bootcamps/conditionals/components/ConditionalReferenceSequence.tsx\n@@\n         <p className=\"cr-sufficiency-lead\"><strong>Necessary means required.</strong> In a conditional relationship, the <strong>necessary condition</strong> is what the sufficient condition requires. Whenever the sufficient condition is true, the necessary condition must be true too. It cannot be missing.</p>\n-        <p>Let's return to the relationship from the last lesson:</p>\n+        <p>Required for what? For the sufficient condition to be true. We are not saying the necessary condition is important, helpful, or usually there. We are saying that <strong>the sufficient condition cannot be true without it.</strong> Even one case with the sufficient condition but without the necessary condition would break the relationship.</p>\n+        <p>The two names describe two roles in the same connection. <strong>Sufficient</strong> asks what is enough to establish something else. <strong>Necessary</strong> asks what that condition cannot be true without. Let's look at our example from both sides.</p>\n+        <h3>What does law-school enrollment require?</h3>\n         <blockquote>If you are enrolled in law school, then you are <strong>a student</strong>.</blockquote>\n-        <p><strong>Being a student</strong> is the required part, introduced here by <strong>then</strong>. If you are enrolled in law school, being a student is certain. You cannot be enrolled without being a student. That is why <strong>being a student is necessary for law-school enrollment</strong>.</p>\n+        <p>In the last lesson, we started with <strong>being enrolled in law school</strong>. That was enough to know you are a student. Now look at what enrollment makes certain: <strong>being a student</strong>. This is the necessary condition, introduced here by <strong>then</strong>.</p>\n+        <p>Try to imagine someone who is enrolled in law school but is not a student. The two descriptions cannot fit together. A person enrolled in law school is one kind of student. You cannot keep the enrollment and take away the studenthood. That is why <strong>being a student is necessary for law-school enrollment</strong>.</p>\n+        <div className=\"nc-role-comparison\" aria-label=\"One relationship described from both sides\">\n+          <div><h4>Enrollment is sufficient for studenthood.</h4><p>Knowing you are enrolled in law school is <strong>enough to establish</strong> that you are a student.</p></div>\n+          <div><h4>Studenthood is necessary for enrollment.</h4><p>Being a student is <strong>required for</strong> being enrolled in law school. Enrollment cannot be true without it.</p></div>\n+        </div>\n+        <p>Those are two descriptions of the same relationship. We have not reversed it or added another rule. And we have not said you actually are enrolled. We are explaining what must be true <strong>if</strong> you are.</p>\n         <section className=\"cr-sufficient-explanation\" aria-label=\"Why a requirement is not necessarily enough\">\n-          <h3>Required doesn't mean enough</h3>\n-          <p>Knowing that a condition is required doesn't, by itself, tell you whether it's enough.</p>\n-          <p>Someone could be a history student without being enrolled in law school. So being a student is required for law-school enrollment without guaranteeing it.</p>\n-          <p>The two conditions have different jobs: <strong>enrollment guarantees being a student; being a student is what enrollment requires.</strong> Knowing only that someone is a student doesn't tell you which subject they study.</p>\n+          <h3>What if all you know is that someone is a student?</h3>\n+          <p>That person meets the requirement. But which subject do they study? They could study law. They could instead be a history student who is not enrolled in law school. Both possibilities fit what we know.</p>\n+          <p>Think back to the groups in the last lesson. Everyone in the law-school group belongs inside the student group. But the student group has room for people outside law school too. Knowing someone is in the larger group does not put them in the smaller one.</p>\n+          <p>So <strong>being a student is required for law-school enrollment without guaranteeing it.</strong> Having the necessary condition leaves enrollment open; missing it rules enrollment out. This is the difference the interaction below will let you compare.</p>\n+          <p>Do not turn that into a rule that a necessary condition can never be sufficient. A condition can have both roles when the relationship supports both. The word <strong>necessary</strong>, by itself, tells you it is required. It does not tell you it is enough.</p>\n         </section>\n@@\n-          <p>These words and phrases can help you recognize a requirement:</p>\n+          <p>An <strong>indicator</strong> is a word or phrase that helps you recognize a condition's role. We used <strong>then</strong> to introduce the required part of our if/then sentence. These Group 2 expressions can also point to what is necessary:</p>\n           <ul>{['only', 'only if', 'only when', 'only where', 'always', 'requires', 'must'].map(word => <li key={word}>{word}</li>)}</ul>\n-          <p>For example, “Law-school enrollment <strong>requires</strong> being a student.” Requires points to <strong>being a student</strong>, the condition that cannot be missing. Read the full relationship; a familiar word alone doesn't tell you what is required.</p>\n+          <h3>Different wording, the same requirement</h3>\n+          <p>Read the sentences below as different ways to describe our law-school relationship. In each one, ask what a person enrolled in law school has to be.</p>\n+          <dl className=\"nc-indicator-examples\">\n+            <div><dt>Requires</dt><dd><blockquote>Being enrolled in law school <strong>requires</strong> being a student.</blockquote><p>What does enrollment require? <strong>Being a student.</strong> Requires is the indicator; being a student is the condition it identifies. They are not the same thing.</p></dd></div>\n+            <div><dt>Must</dt><dd><blockquote>If you are enrolled in law school, you <strong>must</strong> be a student.</blockquote><p>Must makes the certainty explicit: enrollment cannot coexist with not being a student. Here it describes what has to be true, not a task someone has been told to complete.</p></dd></div>\n+            <div><dt>Only</dt><dd><blockquote><strong>Only</strong> students are enrolled in law school.</blockquote><p>This excludes nonstudents from the law-school group. It does not put every student in that group. Being a student remains required; being enrolled remains enough to establish it.</p></dd></div>\n+            <div><dt>Only if</dt><dd><blockquote>You are enrolled in law school <strong>only if</strong> you are a student.</blockquote><p>Only if introduces the requirement: <strong>you are a student</strong>. Read the whole phrase. The if inside only if does not make being a student sufficient.</p></dd></div>\n+            <div><dt>Only when</dt><dd><blockquote>You are enrolled in law school <strong>only when</strong> you are a student.</blockquote><p>On any occasion when enrollment is true, being a student must be true too. This does not say you become enrolled whenever you are a student, or that one condition has to happen later than the other.</p></dd></div>\n+            <div><dt>Always</dt><dd><blockquote>While you are enrolled in law school, you are <strong>always</strong> a student.</blockquote><p>Always allows no exception within the situation described: being enrolled in law school. It does not say every student is enrolled, or that someone remains a student after enrollment ends.</p></dd></div>\n+            <div><dt>Only where</dt><dd><p>This expression restricts places, so use a setting example:</p><blockquote>A seminar takes place <strong>only where</strong> a tutor is present.</blockquote><p>At any place with that seminar, <strong>a tutor must be present</strong>. A tutor could also be somewhere without a seminar. A seminar taking place is sufficient to establish a tutor's presence there; the tutor's presence is necessary for the seminar.</p></dd></div>\n+          </dl>\n+          <h3>Why only if is different from if</h3>\n+          <div className=\"nc-role-comparison\">\n+            <div><h4>If you are enrolled in law school, you are a student.</h4><p><strong>If</strong> identifies enrollment as enough. This is our original relationship.</p></div>\n+            <div><h4>You are enrolled in law school only if you are a student.</h4><p><strong>Only if</strong> identifies being a student as required. This preserves that same relationship.</p></div>\n+          </div>\n+          <p>Now remove only from the second sentence: “You are enrolled in law school <strong>if</strong> you are a student.” That would make being a student enough for law-school enrollment. A history student who is not enrolled in law school shows why that is a different claim.</p>\n+          <p>Whether the sentence starts with the requirement or ends with it, ask the same question: <strong>what cannot be missing if the sufficient condition is true?</strong> Find that complete idea, not just the indicator word. The next example gives you a new relationship to check.</p>\n*** Update File: C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp/src/bootcamps/conditionals/components/sufficient-condition-experience.css\n@@\n .nc-experience { margin-block:2.4rem; padding:clamp(1.2rem,4vw,2.4rem); border-radius:1.25rem; background:var(--sc-ink); color:var(--sc-white); box-shadow:0 18px 42px -26px oklch(20% .035 252 / .5); }\n+.nc-role-comparison { display:grid; grid-template-columns:repeat(2,minmax(0,1fr)); gap:1.5rem; margin-block:1.8rem; padding-block:1.4rem; border-block:1px solid var(--sc-line); }\n+.nc-role-comparison>div { min-width:0; }\n+.cr-sufficiency .nc-role-comparison h4 { font-family:Georgia,serif; font-size:1.25rem; line-height:1.45; color:var(--sc-ink); margin:0 0 .7rem; }\n+.nc-role-comparison p:last-child { margin-bottom:0; }\n+.nc-indicator-examples { margin-block:1.5rem; }\n+.nc-indicator-examples>div { padding-block:1.4rem; border-top:1px solid var(--sc-line); }\n+.nc-indicator-examples dt { font-weight:700; color:var(--sc-ink); }\n+.nc-indicator-examples dd { margin:0; }\n+.nc-indicator-examples blockquote { margin-block:.8rem; }\n+.nc-indicator-examples dd p:last-child { margin-bottom:0; }\n+@media(max-width:640px) { .nc-role-comparison { grid-template-columns:minmax(0,1fr); } }\n*** End Patch"));

In a conditional relationship, the  necessary condition  is what the sufficient condition requires. Whenever the sufficient condition is true, the necessary condition must be true too. It cannot be missing.\n\t\t\t24 container\n\t\t\t\t25 text Required for what? For the sufficient condition to be true. We are not saying the necessary condition is important, helpful, or usually there. We are saying that  the sufficient condition cannot be true without it.  Even one case with the sufficient condition but without the necessary condition would break the relationship.\n\t\t\t26 container\n\t\t\t\t27 text The two names describe two roles in the same connection.  Sufficient  asks what is enough to establish something else.  Necessary  asks what that condition cannot be true without. Let\'s look at our example from both sides.\n\t\t\t28 heading What does law-school enrollment require?, Value: 3\n\t\t\t\t29 text What does law-school enrollment require?\n\t\t\t30 container\n\t\t\t\t31 text If you are enrolled in law school, then you are  a student .\n\t\t\t32 container\n\t\t\t\t33 text In the last lesson, we started with  being enrolled in law school . That was enough to know you are a student. Now look at what enrollment makes certain:  being a student . This is the necessary condition, introduced here by  then .\n\t\t\t34 container\n\t\t\t\t35 text Try to imagine someone who is enrolled in law school but is not a student. The two descriptions cannot fit together. A person enrolled in law school is one kind of student. You cannot keep the enrollment and take away the studenthood. That is why  being a student is necessary for law-school enrollment .\n\t\t\t36 container One relationship described from both sides\n\t\t\t\t37 heading Enrollment is sufficient for studenthood., Value: 4\n\t\t\t\t\t38 text Enrollment is sufficient for studenthood.\n\t\t\t\t39 container\n\t\t\t\t\t40 text Knowing you are enrolled in law school is  enough to establish  that you are a student.\n\t\t\t\t41 heading Studenthood is necessary for enrollment., Value: 4\n\t\t\t\t\t42 text Studenthood is necessary for enrollment.\n\t\t\t\t43 container\n\t\t\t\t\t44 text Being a student is  required for  being enrolled in law school. Enrollment cannot be true without it.\n\t\t\t45 container\n\t\t\t\t46 text Those are two descriptions of the same relationship. We have not reversed it or added another rule. And we have not said you actually are enrolled. We are explaining what must be true  if  you are.\n\t\t\t47 container Why a requirement is not necessarily enough\n\t\t\t\t48 heading What if all you know is that someone is a student?, Value: 3\n\t\t\t\t\t49 text What if all you know is that someone is a student?\n\t\t\t\t50 text That person meets the requirement. But which subject do they study? They could study law. They could instead be a history student who is not enrolled in law school. Both possibilities fit what we know.\n\t\t\t\t51 text Think back to the groups in the last lesson. Everyone in the law-school group belongs inside the student group. But the student group has room for people outside law school too. Knowing someone is in the larger group does not put them in the smaller one.\n\t\t\t\t52 container\n\t\t\t\t\t53 text So  being a student is required for law-school enrollment without guaranteeing it.  Having the necessary condition leaves enrollment open; missing it rules enrollment out. This is the difference the interaction below will let you compare.\n\t\t\t\t54 container\n\t\t\t\t\t55 text Do not turn that into a rule that a necessary condition can never be sufficient. A condition can have both roles when the relationship supports both. The word  necessary , by itself, tells you it is required. It does not tell you it is enough.\n\t\t\t56 container Can you be enrolled without being a student?\n\t\t\t\t57 container\n\t\t\t\t\t58 heading Can you be enrolled without being a student?, Value: 3, ID: :r7:-heading\n\t\t\t\t\t\t59 text Can you be enrolled without being a student?\n\t\t\t\t\t60 text Being a student is required for law-school enrollment. Compare what happens with and without that condition.\n\t\t\t\t61 container Compare the requirement being present or missing\n\t\t\t\t\t62 checkbox A student, Value: 1\n\t\t\t\t\t63 checkbox Not a student, Value: 0\n\t\t\t\t64 container :r7:-reading\n\t\t\t\t\t65 heading Being a student doesn\'t tell us whether you are enrolled in law school., Value: 4\n\t\t\t\t\t\t66 text Being a student doesn\'t tell us whether you are enrolled in law school.\n\t\t\t\t\t67 text You could be enrolled in law school, or you could study something else. Either way, you are a student. Meeting this requirement alone doesn\'t establish enrollment.\n\t\t\t68 container Short explanation of necessity\n\t\t\t\t69 container\n\t\t\t\t\t70 text Watch the explanation\n\t\t\t\t\t71 heading Why the requirement is not enough here, Value: 3\n\t\t\t\t\t\t72 text Why the requirement is not enough here\n\t\t\t\t73 container\n\t\t\t\t\t74 container ID: :r9:, Description: Law-school students and history students both belong to the student group. We used  then  to introduce the required part of our if/then sentence. These Group 2 expressions can also point to what is necessary:\n\t\t\t\t90 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t91 text only\n\t\t\t\t\t92 text only if\n\t\t\t\t\t93 text only when\n\t\t\t\t\t94 text only where\n\t\t\t\t\t95 text always\n\t\t\t\t\t96 text requires\n\t\t\t\t\t97 text must\n\t\t\t\t98 heading Different wording, the same requirement, Value: 3\n\t\t\t\t\t99 text Different wording, the same requirement\n\t\t\t\t100 text The first six sentences describe our law-school relationship. In each one, ask what a person enrolled in law school has to be. Then we\'ll use a place example for only where.\n\t\t\t\t101 definition list\n\t\t\t\t\t102 container Requires\n\t\t\t\t\t\t103 text Requires\n\t\t\t\t\t104 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t105 text Being enrolled in law school \n\t\t\t\t\t\t106 text requires\n\t\t\t\t\t\t107 text  being a student. What does enrollment require? \n\t\t\t\t\t\t108 text Being a student.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t109 text  Requires is the indicator; being a student is the condition it identifies. They are not the same thing.\n\t\t\t\t\t110 container Must\n\t\t\t\t\t\t111 text Must\n\t\t\t\t\t112 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t113 text If you are enrolled in law school, you \n\t\t\t\t\t\t114 text must\n\t\t\t\t\t\t115 text  be a student. Must makes the certainty explicit: enrollment cannot coexist with not being a student. Here it describes what has to be true, not a task someone has been told to complete.\n\t\t\t\t\t116 container Only\n\t\t\t\t\t\t117 text Only\n\t\t\t\t\t118 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t119 text Only\n\t\t\t\t\t\t120 text  students are enrolled in law school. This excludes nonstudents from the law-school group. It does not put every student in that group. Being a student remains required; being enrolled remains enough to establish it.\n\t\t\t\t\t121 container Only if\n\t\t\t\t\t\t122 text Only if\n\t\t\t\t\t123 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t124 text You are enrolled in law school \n\t\t\t\t\t\t125 text only if\n\t\t\t\t\t\t126 text  you are a student. Only if introduces the requirement: \n\t\t\t\t\t\t127 text you are a student\n\t\t\t\t\t\t128 text . Read the whole phrase. The if inside only if does not make being a student sufficient.\n\t\t\t\t\t129 container Only when\n\t\t\t\t\t\t130 text Only when\n\t\t\t\t\t131 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t132 text You are enrolled in law school \n\t\t\t\t\t\t133 text only when\n\t\t\t\t\t\t134 text  you are a student. On any occasion when enrollment is true, being a student must be true too. This does not say you become enrolled whenever you are a student, or that one condition has to happen later than the other.\n\t\t\t\t\t135 container Always\n\t\t\t\t\t\t136 text Always\n\t\t\t\t\t137 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t138 text While you are enrolled in law school, you are \n\t\t\t\t\t\t139 text always\n\t\t\t\t\t\t140 text  a student. Always allows no exception within the situation described: being enrolled in law school. It does not say every student is enrolled, or that someone remains a student after enrollment ends.\n\t\t\t\t\t141 container Only where\n\t\t\t\t\t\t142 text Only where\n\t\t\t\t\t143 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t144 text This expression restricts places, so use a setting example: A seminar takes place \n\t\t\t\t\t\t145 text only where\n\t\t\t\t\t\t146 text  a tutor is present. At any place with that seminar, \n\t\t\t\t\t\t147 text a tutor must be present\n\t\t\t\t\t\t148 text . A tutor could also be somewhere without a seminar. A seminar taking place is sufficient to establish a tutor\'s presence there; the tutor\'s presence is necessary for the seminar.\n\t\t\t\t149 heading Why only if is different from if, Value: 3\n\t\t\t\t\t150 text Why only if is different from if\n\t\t\t\t151 heading If you are enrolled in law school, you are a student., Value: 4\n\t\t\t\t\t152 text If you are enrolled in law school, you are a student.\n\t\t\t\t153 container\n\t\t\t\t\t154 text If  identifies enrollment as enough. [Task 1]\\n"}'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"27c181","wall_time_seconds":1.2969098,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":7004,"output":"Warning: truncated output (original token count: 7004)\\nTotal output lines: 679\\n\\n---\\r\\nname: emil-design-eng\\r\\ndescription: This skill encodes Emil Kowalski\'s philosophy on UI polish, component design, animation decisions, and the invisible details that make software feel great.\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# Design Engineering\\r\\n\\r\\n## Initial Response\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen this skill is first invoked without a specific question, respond only with:\\r\\n\\r\\n> I\'m ready to help you build interfaces that feel right, my knowledge comes from Emil Kowalski\'s design engineering philosophy. If you want to dive even deeper, check out Emil’s course: [animations.dev](https://animations.dev/).\\r\\n\\r\\nDo not provide any other information until the user asks a question.\\r\\n\\r\\nYou are a design engineer with the craft sensibility. You build interfaces where every detail compounds into something that feels right. You understand that in a world where everyone\'s software is good enough, taste is the differentiator.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Core Philosophy\\r\\n\\r\\n### Taste is trained, not innate\\r\\n\\r\\nGood taste is not personal preference. It is a trained instinct: the ability to see beyond the obvious and recognize what elevates. You develop it by surrounding yourself with great work, thinking deeply about why something feels good, and practicing relentlessly.\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen building UI, don\'t just make it work. Study why the best interfaces feel the way they do. Reverse engineer animations. Inspect interactions. Be curious.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Unseen details compound\\r\\n\\r\\nMost details users never consciously notice. That is the point. When a feature functions exactly as someone assumes it should, they proceed without giving it a second thought. That is the goal.\\r\\n\\r\\n> \\"All those unseen details combine to produce something that\'s just stunning, like a thousand barely audible voices all singing in tune.\\" - Paul Graham\\r\\n\\r\\nEvery decision below exists because the aggregate of invisible correctness creates interfaces people love without knowing why.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Beauty is leverage\\r\\n\\r\\nPeople select tools based on the overall experience, not just functionality. Good defaults and good animations are real differentiators. Beauty is underutilized in software. Use it as leverage to stand out.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Review Format (Required)\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen reviewing UI code, you MUST use a markdown table with Before/After columns. Do NOT use a list with \\"Before:\\" and \\"After:\\" on separate lines. Always output an actual markdown table like this:\\r\\n\\r\\n| Before | After | Why |\\r\\n| --- | --- | --- |\\r\\n| `transition: all 300ms` | `transition: transform 200ms ease-out` | Specify exact properties; avoid `all` |\\r\\n| `transform: scale(0)` | `transform: scale(0.95); opacity: 0` | Nothing in the real world appears from nothing |\\r\\n| `ease-in` on dropdown | `ease-out` with custom curve | `ease-in` feels sluggish; `ease-out` gives instant feedback |\\r\\n| No `:active` state on button | `transform: scale(0.97)` on `:active` | Buttons must feel responsive to press |\\r\\n| `transform-origin: center` on popover | `transform-origin: var(--radix-popover-content-transform-origin)` | Popovers should scale from their trigger (not modals — modals stay centered) |\\r\\n\\r\\nWrong format (never do this):\\r\\n\\r\\n```\\r\\nBefore: transition: all 300ms\\r\\nAfter: transition: transform 200ms ease-out\\r\\n────────────────────────────\\r\\nBefore: scale(0)\\r\\nAfter: scale(0.95)\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nCorrect format: A single markdown table with | Before | After | Why | columns, one row per issue found. The \\"Why\\" column briefly explains the reasoning.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The Animation Decision Framework\\r\\n\\r\\nBefore writing any animation code, answer these questions in order:\\r\\n\\r\\n### 1. Should this animate at all?\\r\\n\\r\\n**Ask:** How often will users see this animation?\\r\\n\\r\\n| Frequency                                                   | Decision                     |\\r\\n| ----------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |\\r\\n| 100+ times/day (keyboard shortcuts, command palette toggle) | No animation. Ever.          |\\r\\n| Tens of times/day (hover effects, list navigation)          | Remove or drastically reduce |\\r\\n| Occasional (modals, drawers, toasts)                        | Standard animation           |\\r\\n| Rare/first-time (onboarding, feedback forms, celebrations)  | Can add delight              |\\r\\n\\r\\n**Never animate keyboard-initiated actions.** These actions are repeated hundreds of times daily. Animation makes them feel slow, delayed, and disconnected from the user\'s actions.\\r\\n\\r\\nRaycast has no open/close animation. That is the optimal experience for something used hundreds of times a day.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 2. What is the purpose?\\r\\n\\r\\nEvery animation must have a clear answer to \\"why does this animate?\\"\\r\\n\\r\\nValid purposes:\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Spatial consistency**: toast enters and exits from the same direction, making swipe-to-dismiss feel intuitive\\r\\n- **State indication**: a morphing feedback button shows the state change\\r\\n- **Explanation**: a marketing animation that shows how a feature works\\r\\n- **Feedback**: a button scales down on press, confirming the interface heard the user\\r\\n- **Preventing jarring changes**: elements appearing or disappearing without transition feel broken\\r\\n\\r\\nIf the purpose is just \\"it looks cool\\" and the user will see it often, don\'t animate.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 3. What easing should it use?\\r\\n\\r\\nIs the element entering or exiting?\\r\\n  Yes → ease-out (starts fast, feels responsive)\\r\\n  No →\\r\\n    Is it moving/morphing on screen?\\r\\n      Yes → ease-in-out (natural acceleration/deceleration)\\r\\n    Is it a hover/color change?\\r\\n      Yes → ease\\r\\n    Is it constant motion (marquee, progress bar)?\\r\\n      Yes → linear\\r\\n    Default → ease-out\\r\\n\\r\\n**Critical: use custom easing curves.** The built-in CSS easings are too weak. They lack the punch that makes animations feel intentional.\\r\\n\\r\\n```css\\r\\n/* Strong ease-out for UI interactions */\\r\\n--ease-out: cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1);\\r\\n\\r\\n/* Strong ease-in-out for on-screen movement */\\r\\n--ease-in-out: cubic-bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1);\\r\\n\\r\\n/* iOS-like drawer curve (from Ionic Framework) */\\r\\n--ease-drawer: cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1);\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n**Never use ease-in for UI animations.** It starts slow, which makes the interface feel sluggish and unresponsive. A dropdown with `ease-in` at 300ms _feels_ slower than `ease-out` at the same 300ms, because ease-in delays the initial movement — the exact moment the user is watching most closely.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Easing curve resources:** Don\'t create curves from scratch. Use [easing.dev](https://easing.dev/) or [easings.co](https://easings.co/) to find stronger custom variants of standard easings.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 4. How fast should it be?\\r\\n\\r\\n| Element                  | Duration      |\\r\\n| ------------------------ | ------------- |\\r\\n| Button press feedback    | 100-160ms     |\\r\\n| Tooltips, small popovers | 125-200ms     |\\r\\n| Dropdowns, selects       | 150-250ms     |\\r\\n| Modals, drawers          | 200-500ms     |\\r\\n| Marketing/explanatory    | Can be longer |\\r\\n\\r\\n**Rule: UI animations should stay under 300ms.** A 180ms dropdown feels more responsive than a 400ms one. A faster-spinning spinner makes the app feel like it loads faster, even when the load time is identical.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Perceived performance\\r\\n\\r\\nSpeed in animation is not just about feeling snappy — it directly affects how users perceive your app\'s performance:\\r\\n\\r\\n- A **fast-spinning spinner** makes loading feel faster (same load time, different perception)\\r\\n- A **180ms select** animation feels more responsive than a **400ms** one\\r\\n- **Instant tooltips** after the first one is open (skip delay + skip animation) make the whole toolbar feel faster\\r\\n\\r\\nThe perception of speed matters as much as actual speed. Easing amplifies this: `ease-out` at 200ms _feels_ faster than `ease-in` at 200ms because the user sees immediate movement.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Spring Animations\\r\\n\\r\\nSprings feel more natural than duration-based animations because they simulate real physics. They don\'t have fixed durations — they settle based on physical parameters.\\r\\n\\r\\n### When to use springs\\r\\n\\r\\n- Drag interactions with momentum\\r\\n- Elements that should feel \\"alive\\" (like Apple\'s Dynamic Island)\\r\\n- Gestures that can be interrupted mid-animation\\r\\n- Decorative mouse-tracking interactions\\r\\n\\r\\n### Spring-based mouse interactions\\r\\n\\r\\nTying visual changes directly to mouse position feels artificial because it lacks motion. Use `useSpring` from Motion (formerly Framer Motion) to interpolate value changes with spring-like behavior instead of updating immediately.\\r\\n\\r\\n```jsx\\r\\nimport { useSpring } from \'framer-motion\';\\r\\n\\r\\n// Without spring: feels artificial, instant\\r\\nconst rotation = mouseX * 0.1;\\r\\n\\r\\n// With spring: feels natural, has momentum\\r\\nconst springRotation = useSpring(mouseX * 0.1, {\\r\\n  stiffness: 100,\\r\\n  damping: 10,\\r\\n});\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nThis works because the animation is **decorative** — it doesn\'t serve a function. If this were a functional graph in a banking app, no animation would be better. Know when decoration helps and when it hinders.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Spring configuration\\r\\n\\r\\n**Apple\'s approach (recommended — easier to reason about):**\\r\\n\\r\\n```js\\r\\n{ type: \\"spring\\", duration: 0.5, bounce: 0.2 }\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n**Traditional physics (more control):**\\r\\n\\r\\n```js\\r\\n{ type: \\"spring\\", mass: 1, stiffness: 100, damping: 10 }\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nKeep bounce subtle (0.1-0.3) when used. Avoid bounce in most UI contexts. Use it for drag-to-dismiss and playful interactions.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Interruptibility advantage\\r\\n\\r\\nSprings maintain velocity when interrupted — CSS animations and keyframes restart from zero. This makes springs ideal for gestures users might change mid-motion. When you click an expanded item and quickly press Escape, a spring-based animation smoothly reverses from its current position.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Component Building Principles\\r\\n\\r\\n### Buttons must feel responsive\\r\\n\\r\\nAdd `transform: scale(0.97)` on `:active`. This gives instant feedback, making the UI feel like it is truly listening to the user.\\r\\n\\r\\n```css\\r\\n.button {\\r\\n  transition: transform 160ms ease-out;\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\n.button:active {\\r\\n  transform: scale(0.97);\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nThis applies to any pressable element. The scale should be subtle (0.95-0.98).\\r\\n\\r\\n### Never animate from scale(0)\\r\\n\\r\\nNothing in the real world disappears and reappears completely. Elements animating from `scale(0)` look like they come out of nowhere.\\r\\n\\r\\nStart from `scale(0.9)` or higher, combined with opacity. Even a barely-visible initial scale makes the entrance feel more natural, like a balloon that has a visible shape even when deflated.\\r\\n\\r\\n```css\\r\\n/* Bad */\\r\\n.entering {\\r\\n  transform: scale(0);\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\n/* Good */\\r\\n.entering {\\r\\n  transform: scale(0.95);\\r\\n  opacity: 0;\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n### Make popovers origin-aware\\r\\n\\r\\nPopovers should scale in from their trigger, not from center. The default `transform-origin: center` is wrong for almost every popover. **Exception: modals.** Modals should keep `transform-origin: center` because they are not anchored to a specific trigger — they appear centered in the viewport.\\r\\n\\r\\n```css\\r\\n/* Radix UI */\\r\\n.popover {\\r\\n  transform-origin: var(--radix-popover-content-transform-origin);\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\n/* Base UI */\\r\\n.popover {\\r\\n  transform-origin: var(--transform-origin);\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nWhether the user notices the difference individually does not matter. In the aggregate, unseen details become visible. They compound.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Tooltips: skip delay on subsequent hovers\\r\\n\\r\\nTooltips should delay before appearing to prevent accidental activation. But once one tooltip is open, hovering over adjacent tooltips should open them instantly with no animation. This feels faster without defeating the purpose of the initial delay.\\r\\n\\r\\n```css\\r\\n.tooltip {\\r\\n  transition: transform 125ms ease-out, opacity 125ms ease-out;\\r\\n  transform-origin: var(--transform-origin);\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\n.tooltip[data-starting-style],\\r\\n.tooltip[data-ending-style] {\\r\\n  opacity: 0;\\r\\n  transform: scale(0.97);\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\n/* Skip animation on subsequent tooltips */\\r\\n.tooltip[data-instant] {\\r\\n  transition-duration: 0ms;\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n### Use CSS transitions over keyframes for interruptible UI\\r\\n\\r\\nCSS transitions can be interrupted and retargeted mid-ani…1004 tokens truncated…ip-path: inset(0 0 0 0);\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\n/* Reveal from left to right */\\r\\n.overlay {\\r\\n  clip-path: inset(0 100% 0 0);\\r\\n  transition: clip-path 200ms ease-out;\\r\\n}\\r\\n.button:active .overlay {\\r\\n  clip-path: inset(0 0 0 0);\\r\\n  transition: clip-path 2s linear;\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n### Tabs with perfect color transitions\\r\\n\\r\\nDuplicate the tab list. Style the copy as \\"active\\" (different background, different text color). Clip the copy so only the active tab is visible. Animate the clip on tab change. This creates a seamless color transition that timing individual color transitions can never achieve.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Hold-to-delete pattern\\r\\n\\r\\nUse `clip-path: inset(0 100% 0 0)` on a colored overlay. On `:active`, transition to `inset(0 0 0 0)` over 2s with linear timing. On release, snap back with 200ms ease-out. Add `scale(0.97)` on the button for press feedback.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Image reveals on scroll\\r\\n\\r\\nStart with `clip-path: inset(0 0 100% 0)` (hidden from bottom). Animate to `inset(0 0 0 0)` when the element enters the viewport. Use `IntersectionObserver` or Framer Motion\'s `useInView` with `{ once: true, margin: \\"-100px\\" }`.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Comparison sliders\\r\\n\\r\\nOverlay two images. Clip the top one with `clip-path: inset(0 50% 0 0)`. Adjust the right inset value based on drag position. No extra DOM elements needed, fully hardware-accelerated.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Gesture and Drag Interactions\\r\\n\\r\\n### Momentum-based dismissal\\r\\n\\r\\nDon\'t require dragging past a threshold. Calculate velocity: `Math.abs(dragDistance) / elapsedTime`. If velocity exceeds ~0.11, dismiss regardless of distance. A quick flick should be enough.\\r\\n\\r\\n```js\\r\\nconst timeTaken = new Date().getTime() - dragStartTime.current.getTime();\\r\\nconst velocity = Math.abs(swipeAmount) / timeTaken;\\r\\n\\r\\nif (Math.abs(swipeAmount) >= SWIPE_THRESHOLD || velocity > 0.11) {\\r\\n  dismiss();\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n### Damping at boundaries\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen a user drags past the natural boundary (e.g., dragging a drawer up when already at top), apply damping. The more they drag, the less the element moves. Things in real life don\'t suddenly stop; they slow down first.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Pointer capture for drag\\r\\n\\r\\nOnce dragging starts, set the element to capture all pointer events. This ensures dragging continues even if the pointer leaves the element bounds.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Multi-touch protection\\r\\n\\r\\nIgnore additional touch points after the initial drag begins. Without this, switching fingers mid-drag causes the element to jump to the new position.\\r\\n\\r\\n```js\\r\\nfunction onPress() {\\r\\n  if (isDragging) return;\\r\\n  // Start drag...\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n### Friction instead of hard stops\\r\\n\\r\\nInstead of preventing upward drag entirely, allow it with increasing friction. It feels more natural than hitting an invisible wall.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Performance Rules\\r\\n\\r\\n### Only animate transform and opacity\\r\\n\\r\\nThese properties skip layout and paint, running on the GPU. Animating `padding`, `margin`, `height`, or `width` triggers all three rendering steps.\\r\\n\\r\\n### CSS variables are inheritable\\r\\n\\r\\nChanging a CSS variable on a parent recalculates styles for all children. In a drawer with many items, updating `--swipe-amount` on the container causes expensive style recalculation. Update `transform` directly on the element instead.\\r\\n\\r\\n```js\\r\\n// Bad: triggers recalc on all children\\r\\nelement.style.setProperty(\'--swipe-amount\', `${distance}px`);\\r\\n\\r\\n// Good: only affects this element\\r\\nelement.style.transform = `translateY(${distance}px)`;\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n### Framer Motion hardware acceleration caveat\\r\\n\\r\\nFramer Motion\'s shorthand properties (`x`, `y`, `scale`) are NOT hardware-accelerated. They use `requestAnimationFrame` on the main thread. For hardware acceleration, use the full `transform` string:\\r\\n\\r\\n```jsx\\r\\n// NOT hardware accelerated (convenient but drops frames under load)\\r\\n<motion.div animate={{ x: 100 }} />\\r\\n\\r\\n// Hardware accelerated (stays smooth even when main thread is busy)\\r\\n<motion.div animate={{ transform: \\"translateX(100px)\\" }} />\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nThis matters when the browser is simultaneously loading content, running scripts, or painting. At Vercel, the dashboard tab animation used Shared Layout Animations and dropped frames during page loads. Switching to CSS animations (off main thread) fixed it.\\r\\n\\r\\n### CSS animations beat JS under load\\r\\n\\r\\nCSS animations run off the main thread. When the browser is busy loading a new page, Framer Motion animations (using `requestAnimationFrame`) drop frames. CSS animations remain smooth. Use CSS for predetermined animations; JS for dynamic, interruptible ones.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Use WAAPI for programmatic CSS animations\\r\\n\\r\\nThe Web Animations API gives you JavaScript control with CSS performance. Hardware-accelerated, interruptible, and no library needed.\\r\\n\\r\\n```js\\r\\nelement.animate([{ clipPath: \'inset(0 0 100% 0)\' }, { clipPath: \'inset(0 0 0 0)\' }], {\\r\\n  duration: 1000,\\r\\n  fill: \'forwards\',\\r\\n  easing: \'cubic-bezier(0.77, 0, 0.175, 1)\',\\r\\n});\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n## Accessibility\\r\\n\\r\\n### prefers-reduced-motion\\r\\n\\r\\nAnimations can cause motion sickness. Reduced motion means fewer and gentler animations, not zero. Keep opacity and color transitions that aid comprehension. Remove movement and position animations.\\r\\n\\r\\n```css\\r\\n@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {\\r\\n  .element {\\r\\n    animation: fade 0.2s ease;\\r\\n    /* No transform-based motion */\\r\\n  }\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n```jsx\\r\\nconst shouldReduceMotion = useReducedMotion();\\r\\nconst closedX = shouldReduceMotion ? 0 : \'-100%\';\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n### Touch device hover states\\r\\n\\r\\n```css\\r\\n@media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine) {\\r\\n  .element:hover {\\r\\n    transform: scale(1.05);\\r\\n  }\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nTouch devices trigger hover on tap, causing false positives. Gate hover animations behind this media query.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The Sonner Principles (Building Loved Components)\\r\\n\\r\\nThese principles come from building Sonner (13M+ weekly npm downloads) and apply to any component:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Developer experience is key.** No hooks, no context, no complex setup. Insert `<Toaster />` once, call `toast()` from anywhere. The less friction to adopt, the more people will use it.\\r\\n\\r\\n2. **Good defaults matter more than options.** Ship beautiful out of the box. Most users never customize. The default easing, timing, and visual design should be excellent.\\r\\n\\r\\n3. **Naming creates identity.** \\"Sonner\\" (French for \\"to ring\\") feels more elegant than \\"react-toast\\". Sacrifice discoverability for memorability when appropriate.\\r\\n\\r\\n4. **Handle edge cases invisibly.** Pause toast timers when the tab is hidden. Fill gaps between stacked toasts with pseudo-elements to maintain hover state. Capture pointer events during drag. Users never notice these, and that is exactly right.\\r\\n\\r\\n5. **Use transitions, not keyframes, for dynamic UI.** Toasts are added rapidly. Keyframes restart from zero on interruption. Transitions retarget smoothly.\\r\\n\\r\\n6. **Build a great documentation site.** Let people touch the product, play with it, and understand it before they use it. Interactive examples with ready-to-use code snippets lower the barrier to adoption.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Cohesion matters\\r\\n\\r\\nSonner\'s animation feels satisfying partly because the whole experience is cohesive. The easing and duration fit the vibe of the library. It is slightly slower than typical UI animations and uses `ease` rather than `ease-out` to feel more elegant. The animation style matches the toast design, the page design, the name — everything is in harmony.\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen choosing animation values, consider the personality of the component. A playful component can be bouncier. A professional dashboard should be crisp and fast. Match the motion to the mood.\\r\\n\\r\\n### The opacity + height combination\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen items enter and exit a list (like Family\'s drawer), the opacity change must work well with the height animation. This is often trial and error. There is no formula — you adjust until it feels right.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Review your work the next day\\r\\n\\r\\nReview animations with fresh eyes. You notice imperfections the next day that you missed during development. Play animations in slow motion or frame by frame to spot timing issues that are invisible at full speed.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Asymmetric enter/exit timing\\r\\n\\r\\nPressing should be slow when it needs to be deliberate (hold-to-delete: 2s linear), but release should always be snappy (200ms ease-out). This pattern applies broadly: slow where the user is deciding, fast where the system is responding.\\r\\n\\r\\n```css\\r\\n/* Release: fast */\\r\\n.overlay {\\r\\n  transition: clip-path 200ms ease-out;\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\n/* Press: slow and deliberate */\\r\\n.button:active .overlay {\\r\\n  transition: clip-path 2s linear;\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n## Stagger Animations\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen multiple elements enter together, stagger their appearance. Each element animates in with a small delay after the previous one. This creates a cascading effect that feels more natural than everything appearing at once.\\r\\n\\r\\n```css\\r\\n.item {\\r\\n  opacity: 0;\\r\\n  transform: translateY(8px);\\r\\n  animation: fadeIn 300ms ease-out forwards;\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\n.item:nth-child(1) {\\r\\n  animation-delay: 0ms;\\r\\n}\\r\\n.item:nth-child(2) {\\r\\n  animation-delay: 50ms;\\r\\n}\\r\\n.item:nth-child(3) {\\r\\n  animation-delay: 100ms;\\r\\n}\\r\\n.item:nth-child(4) {\\r\\n  animation-delay: 150ms;\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\n@keyframes fadeIn {\\r\\n  to {\\r\\n    opacity: 1;\\r\\n    transform: translateY(0);\\r\\n  }\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nKeep stagger delays short (30-80ms between items). Long delays make the interface feel slow. Stagger is decorative — never block interaction while stagger animations are playing.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Debugging Animations\\r\\n\\r\\n### Slow motion testing\\r\\n\\r\\nPlay animations at reduced speed to spot issues invisible at full speed. Temporarily increase duration to 2-5x normal, or use browser DevTools animation inspector to slow playback.\\r\\n\\r\\nThings to look for in slow motion:\\r\\n\\r\\n- Do colors transition smoothly, or do you see two distinct states overlapping?\\r\\n- Does the easing feel right, or does it start/stop abruptly?\\r\\n- Is the transform-origin correct, or does the element scale from the wrong point?\\r\\n- Are multiple animated properties (opacity, transform, color) in sync?\\r\\n\\r\\n### Frame-by-frame inspection\\r\\n\\r\\nStep through animations frame by frame in Chrome DevTools (Animations panel). This reveals timing issues between coordinated properties that you cannot see at full speed.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Test on real devices\\r\\n\\r\\nFor touch interactions (drawers, swipe gestures), test on physical devices. Connect your phone via USB, visit your local dev server by IP address, and use Safari\'s remote devtools. In a conditional relationship, the  necessary condition  is what the sufficient condition requires. Whenever the sufficient condition is true, the necessary condition must be true too. It cannot be missing.\n\t\t\t24 container\n\t\t\t\t25 text Required for what? For the sufficient condition to be true. We are not saying the necessary condition is important, helpful, or usually there. We are saying that  the sufficient condition cannot be true without it.  Even one case with the sufficient condition but without the necessary condition would break the relationship.\n\t\t\t26 container\n\t\t\t\t27 text The two names describe two roles in the same connection.  Sufficient  asks what is enough to establish something else.  Necessary  asks what that condition cannot be true without. Let\'s look at our example from both sides.\n\t\t\t28 heading What does law-school enrollment require?, Value: 3\n\t\t\t\t29 text What does law-school enrollment require?\n\t\t\t30 container\n\t\t\t\t31 text If you are enrolled in law school, then you are  a student .\n\t\t\t32 container\n\t\t\t\t33 text In the last lesson, we started with  being enrolled in law school . That was enough to know you are a student. Now look at what enrollment makes certain:  being a student . This is the necessary condition, introduced here by  then .\n\t\t\t34 container\n\t\t\t\t35 text Try to imagine someone who is enrolled in law school but is not a student. The two descriptions cannot fit together. A person enrolled in law school is one kind of student. You cannot keep the enrollment and take away the studenthood. That is why  being a student is necessary for law-school enrollment .\n\t\t\t36 container One relationship described from both sides\n\t\t\t\t37 heading Enrollment is sufficient for studenthood., Value: 4\n\t\t\t\t\t38 text Enrollment is sufficient for studenthood.\n\t\t\t\t39 container\n\t\t\t\t\t40 text Knowing you are enrolled in law school is  enough to establish  that you are a student.\n\t\t\t\t41 heading Studenthood is necessary for enrollment., Value: 4\n\t\t\t\t\t42 text Studenthood is necessary for enrollment.\n\t\t\t\t43 container\n\t\t\t\t\t44 text Being a student is  required for  being enrolled in law school. Enrollment cannot be true without it.\n\t\t\t45 container\n\t\t\t\t46 text Those are two descriptions of the same relationship. We have not reversed it or added another rule. And we have not said you actually are enrolled. We are explaining what must be true  if  you are.\n\t\t\t47 container Why a requirement is not necessarily enough\n\t\t\t\t48 heading What if all you know is that someone is a student?, Value: 3\n\t\t\t\t\t49 text What if all you know is that someone is a student?\n\t\t\t\t50 text That person meets the requirement. But which subject do they study? They could study law. They could instead be a history student who is not enrolled in law school. Both possibilities fit what we know.\n\t\t\t\t51 text Think back to the groups in the last lesson. Everyone in the law-school group belongs inside the student group. But the student group has room for people outside law school too. Knowing someone is in the larger group does not put them in the smaller one.\n\t\t\t\t52 container\n\t\t\t\t\t53 text So  being a student is required for law-school enrollment without guaranteeing it.  Having the necessary condition leaves enrollment open; missing it rules enrollment out. This is the difference the interaction below will let you compare.\n\t\t\t\t54 container\n\t\t\t\t\t55 text Do not turn that into a rule that a necessary condition can never be sufficient. A condition can have both roles when the relationship supports both. The word  necessary , by itself, tells you it is required. It does not tell you it is enough.\n\t\t\t56 container Can you be enrolled without being a student?\n\t\t\t\t57 container\n\t\t\t\t\t58 heading Can you be enrolled without being a student?, Value: 3, ID: :r7:-heading\n\t\t\t\t\t\t59 text Can you be enrolled without being a student?\n\t\t\t\t\t60 text Being a student is required for law-school enrollment. Compare what happens with and without that condition.\n\t\t\t\t61 container Compare the requirement being present or missing\n\t\t\t\t\t62 checkbox A student, Value: 1\n\t\t\t\t\t63 checkbox Not a student, Value: 0\n\t\t\t\t64 container :r7:-reading\n\t\t\t\t\t65 heading Being a student doesn\'t tell us whether you are enrolled in law school., Value: 4\n\t\t\t\t\t\t66 text Being a student doesn\'t tell us whether you are enrolled in law school.\n\t\t\t\t\t67 text You could be enrolled in law school, or you could study something else. Either way, you are a student. We used  then  to introduce the required part of our if/then sentence. These Group 2 expressions can also point to what is necessary:\n\t\t\t\t90 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t91 text only\n\t\t\t\t\t92 text only if\n\t\t\t\t\t93 text only when\n\t\t\t\t\t94 text only where\n\t\t\t\t\t95 text always\n\t\t\t\t\t96 text requires\n\t\t\t\t\t97 text must\n\t\t\t\t98 heading Different wording, the same requirement, Value: 3\n\t\t\t\t\t99 text Different wording, the same requirement\n\t\t\t\t100 text The first six sentences describe our law-school relationship. In each one, ask what a person enrolled in law school has to be. Then we\'ll use a place example for only where.\n\t\t\t\t101 definition list\n\t\t\t\t\t102 container Requires\n\t\t\t\t\t\t103 text Requires\n\t\t\t\t\t104 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t105 text Being enrolled in law school \n\t\t\t\t\t\t106 text requires\n\t\t\t\t\t\t107 text  being a student. What does enrollment require? \n\t\t\t\t\t\t108 text Being a student.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t109 text  Requires is the indicator; being a student is the condition it identifies. They are not the same thing.\n\t\t\t\t\t110 container Must\n\t\t\t\t\t\t111 text Must\n\t\t\t\t\t112 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t113 text If you are enrolled in law school, you \n\t\t\t\t\t\t114 text must\n\t\t\t\t\t\t115 text  be a student. Must makes the certainty explicit: enrollment cannot coexist with not being a student. Here it describes what has to be true, not a task someone has been told to complete.\n\t\t\t\t\t116 container Only\n\t\t\t\t\t\t117 text Only\n\t\t\t\t\t118 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t119 text Only\n\t\t\t\t\t\t120 text  students are enrolled in law school. This excludes nonstudents from the law-school group. It does not put every student in that group. Being a student remains required; being enrolled remains enough to establish it.\n\t\t\t\t\t121 container Only if\n\t\t\t\t\t\t122 text Only if\n\t\t\t\t\t123 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t124 text You are enrolled in law school \n\t\t\t\t\t\t125 text only if\n\t\t\t\t\t\t126 text  you are a student. Only if introduces the requirement: \n\t\t\t\t\t\t127 text you are a student\n\t\t\t\t\t\t128 text . Read the whole phrase. The if inside only if does not make being a student sufficient.\n\t\t\t\t\t129 container Only when\n\t\t\t\t\t\t130 text Only when\n\t\t\t\t\t131 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t132 text You are enrolled in law school \n\t\t\t\t\t\t133 text only when\n\t\t\t\t\t\t134 text  you are a student. On any occasion when enrollment is true, being a student must be true too. This does not say you become enrolled whenever you are a student, or that one condition has to happen later than the other.\n\t\t\t\t\t135 container Always\n\t\t\t\t\t\t136 text Always\n\t\t\t\t\t137 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t138 text While you are enrolled in law school, you are \n\t\t\t\t\t\t139 text always\n\t\t\t\t\t\t140 text  a student. Always allows no exception within the situation described: being enrolled in law school. It does not say every student is enrolled, or that someone remains a student after enrollment ends.\n\t\t\t\t\t141 container Only where\n\t\t\t\t\t\t142 text Only where\n\t\t\t\t\t143 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t144 text This expression restricts places, so use a setting example: A seminar takes place \n\t\t\t\t\t\t145 text only where\n\t\t\t\t\t\t146 text  a tutor is present. At any place with that seminar, \n\t\t\t\t\t\t147 text a tutor must be present\n\t\t\t\t\t\t148 text . A tutor could also be somewhere without a seminar. A seminar taking place is sufficient to establish a tutor\'s presence there; the tutor\'s presence is necessary for the seminar.\n\t\t\t\t149 heading Why only if is different from if, Value: 3\n\t\t\t\t\t150 text Why only if is different from if\n\t\t\t\t151 heading If you are enrolled in law school, you are a student., Value: 4\n\t\t\t\t\t152 text If you are enrolled in law school, you are a student.\n\t\t\t\t153 container\n\t\t\t\t\t154 text If  identifies enrollment as enough. This is our original relationship.\n\t\t\t\t155 heading You are enrolled in law school only if you are a student., Value: 4\n\t\t\t\t\t156 text You are enrolled in law school only if you are a student.\n\t\t\t\t157 container\n\t\t\t\t\t158 text Only if  identifies being a student as required. This preserves that same relationship.\n\t\t\t\t159 container\n\t\t\t\t\t160 text Now remove only from the second sentence: “You are enrolled in law school  if  you are a student.” That would make being a student enough for law-school enrollment. A history student who is not enrolled in law school shows why that is a different claim.\n\t\t\t\t161 container\n\t\t\t\t\t162 text Whether the sentence starts with the requirement or ends with it, ask the same question:  what cannot be missing if the sufficient condition is true? For any interaction that can be triggered rapidly (adding toasts, toggling states), transitions produce smoother results.\\r\\n\\r\\n```css\\r\\n/* Interruptible - good for UI */\\r\\n.toast {\\r\\n  transition: transform 400ms ease;\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\n/* Not interruptible - avoid for dynamic UI */\\r\\n@keyframes slideIn {\\r\\n  from {\\r\\n    transform: translateY(100%);\\r\\n  }\\r\\n  to {\\r\\n    transform: translateY(0);\\r\\n  }\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n### Use blur to mask imperfect transitions\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen a crossfade between two states feels off despite trying different easings and durations, add subtle `filter: blur(2px)` during the transition.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Why blur works:** Without blur, you see two distinct objects during a crossfade — the old state and the new state overlapping. This looks unnatural. Blur bridges the visual gap by blending the two states together, tricking the eye into perceiving a single smooth transformation instead of two objects swapping.\\r\\n\\r\\nCombine blur with scale-on-press (`scale(0.97)`) for a polished button state transition:\\r\\n\\r\\n```css\\r\\n.button {\\r\\n  transition: transform 160ms ease-out;\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\n.button:active {\\r\\n  transform: scale(0.97);\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\n.button-content {\\r\\n  transition: filter 200ms ease, opacity 200ms ease;\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\n.button-content.transitioning {\\r\\n  filter: blur(2px);\\r\\n  opacity: 0.7;\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nKeep blur under 20px. Heavy blur is expensive, especially in Safari.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Animate enter states with @starting-style\\r\\n\\r\\nThe modern CSS way to animate element entry without JavaScript:\\r\\n\\r\\n```css\\r\\n.toast {\\r\\n  opacity: 1;\\r\\n  transform: translateY(0);\\r\\n  transition: opacity 400ms ease, transform 400ms ease;\\r\\n\\r\\n  @starting-style {\\r\\n    opacity: 0;\\r\\n    transform: translateY(100%);\\r\\n  }\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nThis replaces the common React pattern of using `useEffect` to set `mounted: true` after initial render. Use `@starting-style` when browser support allows; fall back to the `data-mounted` attribute pattern otherwise.\\r\\n\\r\\n```jsx\\r\\n// Legacy pattern (still works everywhere)\\r\\nuseEffect(() => {\\r\\n  setMounted(true);\\r\\n}, []);\\r\\n// <div data-mounted={mounted}>\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n## CSS Transform Mastery\\r\\n\\r\\n### translateY with percentages\\r\\n\\r\\nPercentage values in `translate()` are relative to the element\'s own size. Use `translateY(100%)` to move an element by its own height, regardless of actual dimensions. This is how Sonner positions toasts and how Vaul hides the drawer before animating in.\\r\\n\\r\\n```css\\r\\n/* Works regardless of drawer height */\\r\\n.drawer-hidden {\\r\\n  transform: translateY(100%);\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\n/* Works regardless of toast height */\\r\\n.toast-enter {\\r\\n  transform: translateY(-100%);\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nPrefer percentages over hardcoded pixel values. They are less error-prone and adapt to content.\\r\\n\\r\\n### scale() scales children too\\r\\n\\r\\nUnlike `width`/`height`, `scale()` also scales an element\'s children. When scaling a button on press, the font size, icons, and content scale proportionally. This is a feature, not a bug.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 3D transforms for depth\\r\\n\\r\\n`rotateX()`, `rotateY()` with `transform-style: preserve-3d` create real 3D effects in CSS. Orbiting animations, coin flips, and depth effects are all possible without JavaScript.\\r\\n\\r\\n```css\\r\\n.wrapper {\\r\\n  transform-style: preserve-3d;\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\n@keyframes orbit {\\r\\n  from {\\r\\n    transform: translate(-50%, -50%) rotateY(0deg) translateZ(72px) rotateY(360deg);\\r\\n  }\\r\\n  to {\\r\\n    transform: translate(-50%, -50%) rotateY(360deg) translateZ(72px) rotateY(0deg);\\r\\n  }\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n### transform-origin\\r\\n\\r\\nEvery element has an anchor point from which transforms execute. The default is center. Set it to match where the trigger lives for origin-aware interactions.\\r\\n\\r\\n## clip-path for Animation\\r\\n\\r\\n`clip-path` is not just for shapes. It is one of the most powerful animation tools in CSS.\\r\\n\\r\\n### The inset shape\\r\\n\\r\\n`clip-path: inset(top right bottom left)` defines a rectangular clipping region. Each value \\"eats\\" into the element from that side.\\r\\n\\r\\n```css\\r\\n/* Fully hidden from right */\\r\\n.hidden {\\r\\n  clip-path: inset(0 100% 0 0);\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\n/* Fully visible
